fields.Q1:
WHAT IS STANDING AROUND THIS ROOM MADE OF?**
Stone block — two courses of rectangular masonry, dry-laid, no render or facing. But only on the north side, and only under magnification. At 1:1 it is a black bar.
fields.Q1_WHY: The bars at y=200–231 resolve, at 22× brightness, into two rows of rectangular blocks with a joint line between them (`/tmp/wallbarW.png`, `/tmp/wallbarE.png`). Unmagnified, that region has **min 1, max 22, mean 6.0, median 5** across its whole 700 px length. The ground immediately below it runs **min 2, max 56, mean 21.2**. Its internal detail — the local high-pass deviation — measures **1.0–1.24 grey levels**. The material identity lives in about five sRGB codes off black.
fields.Q2:
SOLID MASS, OR FLAT PATTERN?**
**Solid mass — but only for about one-sixth of the perimeter. Everywhere else, neither: the room is bounded by a line.**

The north bar has genuine thickness: one 32 px cell of it, with two courses and a diagonal fracture through the corner blocks at x≈410–440. West, east and south have no wall body at all. At the south edge, x=400: y=764 is (14,12,11), it darkens to (5,5,5) at y=772–773, and at y=774 it is (12,12,17). Ground, a 2 px dark line, void. Same at the west edge (x=56, a single dark line at value 3, with luminance ≈9 on both sides of it) and the east (x=727). I built a texture-energy map of the whole frame (`/tmp/tex.png`): the only non-ground structure anywhere in the image is those two north bars.
fields.Q3:
WHERE EXACTLY DOES THE GROUND STOP?**
South edge, x=400: the ground vignettes down over **10 px** (y=764→773, RGB 14,12,11 → 5,5,5), then **steps up** at y=774 to (12,12,17). The transition is one row wide and it goes the wrong way — the field outside is brighter and bluer than the ground's own last row. North edge, x=470: ground at y=258–261 is (33,28,27), a 4 px dark line at y=262–265, then ground again at y=266. Same treatment in every direction: an 8–10 px darkening, a 2–4 px line, done.
fields.Q4:
WHAT IS HOLDING THIS PLACE TOGETHER?**
**NOTHING.** No rope, no pin, no driven wedge, no salvaged timber, no bracing, no shoring, no lintel, no capping course. I magnified the full length of both bars at 22–24×. What is there: a diagonal fracture at x≈410–440, near-vertical jagged cracks at x≈530 and x≈595, and about fourteen small pale blobs (detected as local maxima at y=204–216 across x=65–571) that read as loose stones or skulls sitting on the top surface. All of that is damage or debris. None of it is holding anything. There is nothing in the image I could cut.
fields.Q5:
BUILT, OR REPEATED?**
**Repeated.** Correlating each normalised 32×32 wall cell against every other: mean **0.455**, 90th percentile 0.697, max **0.877** (x=120 vs x=440). By comparison, mid-room ground rows score 0.033–0.142 mean. More specifically: I profiled each wall cell for its darkest interior row. **Rows 214–215 come up in 13 of ~20 cells** — the same mortar course, at the same height within the cell, ruled straight across 700 px of wall. That is a stamp, not a bond.
fields.Q6:
WOULD YOU BELIEVE THIS SHIPPED?**
**NO.** A commercial game does not ship a room with walls on one side.

Merely competent, or genuinely good? Neither. The standing structure is below competent. The block art itself, viewed magnified, is competent — plausible masonry, real fractures, plausible debris — but it is delivered at a brightness where none of that reaches the player, on one side of four.
fields.Q7:
WHAT CAN YOU ACTUALLY SEE AT 1:1?**
Legible at 1:1 on the standing surfaces: **that a darker horizontal bar exists**, roughly where a wall would be, and four or five faint pale specks on it. That is the complete list. No stone. No joint. No course. No edge. No corner. No fracture — the corner fracture at x≈410–440 is the single largest feature on the wall and I could not see it at 1:1.

Only under magnification: the two-course bond, the mortar joint at y=214–215, the block divisions, the three cracks, the pale blobs as objects rather than specks.

Does it change with distance from the figure? **Barely, and that is itself the problem.** At matched distance ~260 px from the light: wall (450,228) = (12,9,8), (500,225) = (6,5,5); ground at the same radius (408,742) = (20,16,14), (160,487) = (21,16,13). The wall reads at roughly half the ground's value at every radius. The only wall pixels anywhere in the frame above value 16 are at x=312–480 — the corridor mouth, the one spot the torch reaches. Everywhere else the wall never rises off the floor of the scale.
fields.Q8:
ANYTHING YOUR EYE KEEPS RETURNING TO?**
Two things.

**The mortar line at y=214–215.** It is the darkest interior row in 13 of ~20 wall cells, at the identical height in each, running unbroken from x=23 to x=726. A single ruled line through 700 px of masonry, dead centre in every cell. Once seen it does not stop being a stencil.

**The blank rectangle at x=343–376, y=200–265.** West of the corridor mouth, the wall simply stops one cell short. At y=210 and y=215, x=348–375 reads (14,14,18) — the blank fill, not the wall's (4,4,4). On the east side the wall runs flush to the corridor edge (bar starts x=439, corridor edge x=437). One shoulder of the doorway has a wall; the other has a hole.
fields.Q9:
WHAT IS BEYOND THE WALLS?**
**Not darkness.** It is a flat slate-blue field at RGB (6,7,11)–(11,12,16), and it is *brighter* than the ground's own perimeter (5,5,5 at the south edge). Its statistics: standard deviation **0.64** over a 150×60 sample, local high-pass **0.21**. That is a painted backdrop, not space.

At 30× it does have content — soft cloudy blobs and thin branching dark lines, like cracks or roots (`/tmp/void_nw.png`). At 1:1 none of it exists. And it is the *same field everywhere*: north of the wall, west of the room, south of the room, and flanking the corridor for its entire 260 px length where side walls should be. Whatever it is meant to represent, it is presented as one undifferentiated substance surrounding the room on all sides, which means it cannot carry any of the meanings the question offers. It is not more of the same stuff, not empty space, not another room. It is the absence of a decision.
fields.Q10:
COULD YOU TELL A WAY THROUGH WITHOUT WALKING INTO IT?**
**Yes — found it, read it as a passage.** x=377–437 (two cells), running north from y=262 past y=0.

What made the difference: the **ground texture continues through it**. The masonry grid runs up the strip unbroken, and it sits at a higher value than everything beside it (y=245: 16–28 inside, dropping to 12 at x=376 and 9 at x=438). It also runs off the top of the frame rather than terminating, which is the real tell — a notch would close.

The credit belongs entirely to the ground. Nothing bounds this passage. Its two edges are single 1 px dark lines against blank field for the whole run. From y=200 northward there is no wall on either side of it — it is a plank of floor laid across nothing. It reads as a passage in spite of the standing structure, not because of it.
fields.Q11:
HAS ANYTHING HAPPENED TO THIS STRUCTURE?**
Cracked and shedding, never touched. Three fractures — one diagonal through the corner blocks at the corridor mouth (x≈410–440), two near-vertical at x≈530 and x≈595 — each cutting cleanly through both courses. About fourteen pale objects scattered along the top surface. No repair of any kind anywhere on it.

I read that as damage without response, which for a place held for four hundred years by people who are extremely good at fixing things is the wrong story. The orcs' line runs through this room. This wall has been cracked open beside a doorway and nobody has driven a single pin into it.
fields.Q12:
THE DARKER BAND — WALL TOP OR GROUND?**
The band is **y=234–265**, one cell tall, spanning x=56–727. Sequence from the figure outward: ground (mean 21.2) → band (mean 13.5) → wall bar (mean 6.0) → field (~9).

**It is ground. Lit ground.** What decided it: it sits on the ground's own light-falloff curve and the wall does not. At (450,250), d=241, it is (30,26,26); the ground at (408,742), d=255, is (20,16,14); the wall at (450,228), d=262, is (12,9,8). The band tracks the ground and diverges from the wall. It also has no top-edge highlight, casts no shadow onto the ground, and — decisively — the same y-band **is** visibly ground inside the corridor (x=377–437 is fully masonry-textured through y=234–265), while being blank 40 px to either side. Same row, same lighting, masonry in the middle, nothing on the flanks.

**One continuous surface. No breaks.** I detrended the band's column profile with a 61 px window: seam residual **std 0.30, max 0.84 grey levels** over x=60–340. The ground one cell below, same test: **std 3.08, max 13.8**. There is not a single cell division in it anywhere along 670 px. Its local high-pass is **0.32** — statistically indistinguishable from the empty field's 0.21.

So the honest reading: a 670×32 px rectangle of ground, lit correctly, with nothing drawn on it.

---
fields.CULL: Three of four walls do not exist — the ground ends at a 2 px line into flat blue.
fields.FLIP LIST:
- Build the wall on all four sides. West (x=56), east (x=727) and south (y=773) currently end in a 1–3 px dark line with no mass; give them the same one-cell body the north has.
- Raise the wall's tonal range. It sits at mean 6 / median 5 / max 22 against ground at mean 21 / max 56 at identical light radius. Nothing on it — not the two-course bond, not the corner fracture — is visible at 1:1.
- Break the mortar line at y=214–215. It is the darkest interior row in 13 of ~20 cells at the identical height; offset the course per cell or vary the bond.
- Draw the band at y=234–265, or delete it. 670×32 px of lit ground with zero texture and zero cell seams (high-pass 0.32 vs the floor's 2.76), while the same row inside the corridor x=377–437 is fully drawn.
- Close the hole at x=343–376, y=200–265 — the wall stops one cell short of the corridor's west shoulder while running flush to the east shoulder at x=439.

What I'd watch next: the block art itself is fine. Every finding above is a delivery failure — brightness, coverage, and one stamped joint. Fix the exposure and the missing three sides and you may find the material was never the problem.

*Model: Claude Opus 5 (1M context)*
